stories.headline: Rams' Alaric Jackson has suspension cut to 1 game following appeal
stories.summary: Alaric Jackson's suspension for punching Bradley Chubb after Monday night's game between the Bills and Rams was reduced from two games to one.
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- Alaric Jackson's suspension for punching Bradley Chubb after Monday night's game between the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams was reduced from two games to one, the NFL said Wednesday.

The Rams' left tackle had appealed Tuesday's ruling by the league. Hearing officer Derrick Brooks, who was jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFL Players Association, heard the appeal and reduced the punishment to one game.

The league initially said Jackson violated Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship," when he struck Chubb following the Rams' 37-34 overtime loss in Los Angeles on Monday.

"Have to make better decisions than that," Rams coach Sean McVay said Tuesday.

Jackson now will sit out only the Rams' Week 6 game against the Arizona Cardinals. David Quessenberry will start in his place, McVay said Tuesday.

In a scene captured by ESPN's cameras, Jackson stood near midfield following Monday's game while exchanging jerseys with Bills defensive lineman Deone Walker when Chubb said something to him. Jackson then walked toward Chubb before punching the linebacker in the face with his right hand.

On Wednesday, Chubb told reporters that he initiated the conversation with Jackson.

"I've heard I was talking about his mom," Chubb said. "That's not true at all. I said: 'We're gonna see y'all's ass again. And when we see you again, all that chipping ain't gonna save you. That tight end and guard is not going to save you.' He said, 'What'd you say?' I said, 'That chip's not gonna save you. The guard's not gonna save you.' And then boom."

Chubb said he hasn't heard from Jackson since the incident.

"We're going to learn from it," Chubb said. "Me personally, I learned I'm either going to have my hands up or wear a helmet."

This is Jackson's second NFL suspension. He sat out for two games in 2024 for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy.

ESPN's Nick Suss contributed to this report.

stories.headline: AFL trade and free agency grades - Every club's report card from the 2026 transfer period
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL trade and free agency period is over. Some teams improved, some stagnated, and others, well, got worse. Here's how every team fared over the last two weeks.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL trade and free agency period is complete. Some teams improved, some have stagnated, and others, well, seemed to have gotten worse.

READ: Every player move from the 2026 off-season

Here's how every team fared over the last two weeks:

Adelaide
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Jordon Butts, Luke Pedlar

2026 draft selections: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92

I'm not sure what the Crows' gameplan was this trade and free agency period, but it's fair to say the club sat on its hands and did next to nothing. Losing key defender Jordon Butts to the Bulldogs obviously weakens them, while just one draft selection inside the top 30 is unlikely to provide much immediate support. Adelaide's list profile remains fine, and maybe they will surprise us all in 2027, but you just get the sense so many other clubs have passed them by over the last two weeks.

Grade: F

Brisbane
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Lachie Neale, Sam Marshall, Will McLachlan, Keidean Coleman

2026 draft selections: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97

The Lions were the biggest winners of last year's off-season (and season!), but this year was a different story. All year it seemed a formality they would lose the services of dual Brownlow Medal winner Lachie Neale, who ultimately signed with Collingwood as a free agent. They also waved goodbye to Keidean Coleman and Sam Marshall, two players who had struggled to crack the best 23 of late. No picks inside the top 20 would be concerning for 17 other clubs, but the Lions still have so much young talent at their disposal and are primed to challenge again in 2027.

Grade: C-

Carlton
Incoming: Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield

Outgoing: Hudson O'Keeffe, Flynn Riley

2026 draft selections: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90

The Blues addressed two areas of weakness this off-season. The addition of free agent Joel Amartey provides spearhead Harry McKay with a stable forward line partner, while the Lachie Whitfield signing offers run, experience, and a kick-first option off halfback, the perfect piece to fit into Josh Fraser's system. Carlton really didn't give up much to land Whitfield, either. And barring Essendon taking a stab at talented father-son prospect Cody Walker with pick No. 1, the club has also ensured it has enough draft capital to match any bids that will come for him.

Grade: A

Collingwood
Incoming: Lachie Neale, Jesse Hogan, Flynn Riley

Outgoing: Scott Pendlebury

2026 draft selections: 11, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88

The Magpies had been crying out for a true inside midfielder, and they landed arguably the best in the competition in Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow Medal winner is an elite ball winner and clearance player, and should perfectly complement superstar Nick Daicos. Collingwood also signed Jesse Hogan, a man that won the Coleman Medal just two years ago, and gave up virtually nothing for him. The loss of champion Scott Pendlebury obviously stings, but you have to feel this club is in a stronger position now than it was two weeks ago.

Grade: A

Essendon
Incoming: Jack Bowes, Keidean Coleman

Outgoing: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley

2026 draft selections: 1, 17, 25, 80

Former skipper Zach Merrett finally got his wish of a fresh start at the Hawks, while fellow experienced player Jordan Ridley also departs the club for the Cats. The additions of Jack Bowes and Keidean Coleman are fine, but are either going to be difference makers in a side that's been languishing at the bottom of the ladder for several years? I'm not so sure. The only saving grace for the Bombers is that they hold pick No. 1. They simply have to make the most of that selection.

Grade: D

Fremantle
Incoming: Dom Bedendo

Outgoing: Nathan O'Driscoll

2026 draft selections: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96

The Dockers were incredibly quiet during the trade and free agency window, but that's not exactly a bad thing. Remember, if not for Will Ashcroft and Logan Morris, Fremantle win the 2026 premiership. There was absolutely no reason for the Dockers to panic and overpay for someone after their Grand Final heartbreak, instead, this club, with its plethora of youth and talent, should feel as if it can contend for years to come. Trust the process and go again in 2027.

Grade: C

Geelong
Incoming: Toby Greene, Jordan Ridley, Rowan Marshall

Outgoing: Jack Bowes

2026 draft selections: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93

Every year the Cats just find a way to bring big names through the door, and 2026 was no exception. Rowan Marshall was tipped to join 12 months ago and finally makes the move from St Kilda to bolster the club's ruck stocks. Toby Greene adds class, experience, and unrivalled goal-kicking nous to the forward line. Jordan Ridley is a stable and still wildly underrated defensive asset. The best part? To land this trio the club only had to give up midfield depth piece Jack Bowes, and some draft capital. They won't be much of a feature at the upcoming draft, but they don't have to be. These Cats are in win-now mode.

Grade: A

Gold Coast Suns
Incoming: Scott Pendlebury, Aidan Schubert, Sam Butler

Outgoing: Ben King

2026 draft selections: 8, 85

Scott Pendlebury might be a champion of the game, but there's no denying the Suns just got worse. The addition of 38-year-old Pendlebury doesn't outweigh the seismic loss of spearhead Ben King, a man who has booted 230 goals over the last four seasons. How do they replace him? Perhaps it's the incoming Aidan Schubert, but he's years away from having a real impact. Making matters worse, it seems Brownlow medallist Matt Rowell is likely to request a trade back to Victoria at the end of next season. This club is in a real precarious spot right now. A penny for Christian Petracca's thoughts...

Grade: C-

GWS Giants
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Toby Greene, Kieren Briggs, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield

2026 draft selections: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86

Just two years ago Toby Greene, Kieren Briggs, Jesse Hogan, and Lachie Whitfield were probably four of the Giants' most important players. None of them remain at the club after an action-packed trade and free agency window, with GWS instead opting to clear out and trust the youth underneath. It's a move that will either make the Giants look like geniuses or total fools, but even those who are incredibly bullish about the approach would concede there is likely to be some pain on the immediate horizon.

Grade: D

Hawthorn
Incoming: Zach Merrett, Ben King, Josh Goater

Outgoing: Finn Maginness, Aidan Schubert, Sam Butler, Bodie Ryan

2026 draft selections: 29, 37, 71, 94

The Hawks should probably be the 2027 flag favourites after a whirlwind two weeks that's seen them finally land former Essendon skipper Zach Merrett, as well as Ben King. Merrett adds depth, experience, and A-grade ball use to Hawthorn's midfield group, while King provides a focal point in attack, taking the burden off the ageing Jack Gunston. Sure, Hawthorn gave up some depth, but their best 23 has improved out of sight and they still have draft collateral over the next few years to ensure talent keeps coming through the door.

Grade: A+

Melbourne
Incoming: Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, Bodie Ryan

Outgoing: Jack Viney, Trent Rivers

2026 draft selections: 4, 14, 48, 52

Just about everyone panicked when the Demons farewelled premiership heroes Christian Petracca and Clayton Oliver last year, and look how that turned out. This club seems to have a plan for the future and it isn't prepared to compromise on what it wants. Melbourne has nailed its draft picks in recent times and with selections four and 14 this year, you'd expect two more highly talented prospects to join the ranks. Who knows if Zane Duursma will work out, but they've landed him for a fraction of what the Kangaroos gave up at the draft three years ago. It's a low risk punt worth taking.

Grade: C

North Melbourne
Incoming: Nick Blakey

Outgoing: Zane Duursma, Josh Goater

2026 draft selections: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84

Credit to the Kangaroos, they finally landed a big name. The only problem is I'm not sure Nick Blakey is the superstar many are claiming. There's no doubt Blakey will add drive and dash off halfback, but is he the player you look to in the closing stages of a tight game? North also gave up a truckload of future draft capital to get him through the door which will hurt them in the coming years. And then there's the Zane Duursma fiasco. Losing a player the club invested pick No. 4 in just three years ago is an unmitigated disaster. With no selections inside the top 30 this year, it will be a rare draft without the Roos being a major player.

Grade: C+

Port Adelaide
Incoming: Luke Pedlar

Outgoing: Zak Butters

2026 draft selections: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65

You're never going to feel great when a player of Zak Butters' class and calibre walks out the door, but the silver lining for Port Adelaide is that Dougie Cochrane should be set to walk back in. The academy talent is the consensus best player in the upcoming draft and the Power are in a position to match any bids on their man. Expect Port to be heavily involved in the draft over the next couple of years as they look to rebuild around the likes of Cochrane, Connor Rozee, and Jason Horne-Francis.

Grade: B

Richmond
Incoming: Kieren Briggs, Nathan O'Driscoll

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 2, 5, 44, 81

The Tigers found Toby Nankervis' successor in Kieren Briggs, who crosses from the Giants as a free agent. That's a nice win. Nathan O'Driscoll was unable to find a place in Fremantle's best team of late but should receive far more opportunity in the black and yellow jumper in 2027. Richmond has two more picks inside the top five, though they are likely to be shuffled down a few spots with bid matching on Dougie Cochrane and Cody Walker, and they simply must nail them. Even still, this side will remain incredibly young in 2027.

Grade: C

St Kilda
Incoming: Sam Marshall

Outgoing: Rowan Marshall

2026 draft selections: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87

The Saints went all-in last year, signing Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Liam Ryan, and Sam Flanders. They weren't nearly as busy this off-season, and few expected them to be. Long-time ruck Rowan Marshall departs the club for the Cats, while Sam Marshall joins and should bolster their midfield stocks. Outside of that, St Kilda will be hoping to cash in with their two first round draft selections. If not, it could spell the end of Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera's tenure. This team wouldn't want to be starting 2027 slowly...

Grade: C

Sydney Swans
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Joel Amartey, Nick Blakey

2026 draft selections: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95

Two best 23 players departed the Swans this past fortnight with halfback Nick Blakey being traded to the Kangaroos and key forward Joel Amartey signing with the Blues as a free agent. Don't forget, Callum Mills is unlikely to suit up for the entire year after suffering an ACL injury during this year's finals campaign. That's three best 23 players to replace! Who knows what's happening with Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner? Swans fans will be praying for a hit with pick No. 6 at the upcoming draft to soften the blow.

Grade: C-

West Coast Eagles
Incoming: Jack Viney, Trent Rivers

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82

It's clear the Eagles don't want to take the same approach as the Tigers and rely solely on the kids. Instead, they're continuing to add experienced pieces around their young talent in an effort to ease the rebuild and avoid a nosedive in morale. Jack Viney and Trent Rivers add premiership experience to the club and they haven't had to give up too much to get them. West Coast will feature prominently at November's draft with pick No. 3, 23, as well as a compensation pick in the likely scenario that the club's first selection is pushed back by a bid.

Grade: C+

Western Bulldogs
Incoming: Jordon Butts, Finn Maginness, Hudson O'Keeffe, Zak Butters

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91

The Bulldogs now possess the most dynamic midfield trio in the game with Zak Butters joining skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in the red, white, and blue. It's a marquee signing for Luke Beveridge's team that simply has to put them into premiership contention. Jordon Butts also joins the club and will bolster what's traditionally been a weaker defensive unit. Don't forget about key forward star Sam Darcy, who will return from a season-ending ACL injury.

Grade: A+

stories.headline: Ducks rookie dons No. 95, channels Lightning McQueen in NHL debut
stories.summary: After a draft night trip to Disneyland to meet Lightning McQueen, the "Cars" synergy came full circle for the Ducks rookie's NHL debut.
stories.body:
Roger McQueen made his NHL debut for the Anaheim Ducks on Tuesday night. He brought inevitable references to the Pixar classic "Cars" with him.

When McQueen was drafted 10th overall in 2025, the Ducks presented him with a No. 95 jersey -- a reference to the car number of Lightning McQueen, the Owen Wilson-voiced protagonist of the "Cars" movies. After he was selected, the McQueen family went to the 55th floor of The Ritz-Carlton in Los Angeles to board a helicopter and fly to Disneyland in nearby Anaheim, where Roger McQueen met Lightning McQueen.

McQueen got the call Monday night that he would be elevated from the AHL to play for the Ducks.

"I thought he got better in camp as he went along. He was one of those guys that would be pushing for a job," coach Joel Quenneville said of the center. "Roger's got some upside in what could be a really nice career."

On Tuesday night, before the Ducks' home game against Calgary Flames, McQueen took his customary rookie lap to start warmups -- wearing No. 95 and sans helmet -- while the arena speakers blared "Real Gone" by Sheryl Crow. While not a staple of arena rock playlists, it was wholly appropriate here: "Real Gone" is the opening track from the "Cars" soundtrack album and was featured in the film.

McQueen played 11:26 in his NHL debut with no points and a shot on goal. It wasn't a memorable night for the Ducks as they lost to the moribund Flames 4-2 in front of a sellout crowd.

One game down, many more to go for McQueen. When he was drafted, Roger's father Scott McQueen said that the "Cars" connection intensifies the spotlight on the young center as he begins his career.

"I think everybody kind of wants to fly under the radar and you know, and just play," Scott said via the CBC. "He wants to prove himself as a player and not so much, you know, as a Disney character."

stories.headline: When can Kimi Antonelli win the F1 title? Earliest date, points needed and remaining races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Max Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant drive at Singapore GP

- Lewis Hamilton calls Singapore GP strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: The UFC's flyweights are hot again - is Lone'er Kavanagh the next star?
stories.summary: Could a breakout win at UFC 333 propel Britain's Lone'er Kavanagh into the flyweight title picture?
stories.body:
The fighting life of a UFC flyweight was once an unenvied one.

Constant uncertainty over the future of the division, a lack of big pay-per-view interest and an unfortunate routine of far too many fighters getting cut for the weight class to sustain itself were just some of the problems that characterised the modern era. UFC president Dana White put it in simple terms, saying after Demetrious Johnson's UFC exit in 2018 that "people didn't care" about the flyweights. Even Olympic gold medalist and former two-division champion Henry Cejudo struggled to see how the flyweight division would continue as a part of the UFC, with his own brash persona and entertaining title defences pivotal to maintaining awareness of the division.

Much has changed since the days of Cejudo though, and the flyweights now have a genuine claim to being one of the most exciting divisions in the whole of the UFC. And one man at the forefront of that charge is another promising fighting talent from across the Atlantic, with England's Lone'er Kavanagh enjoying a rise like few others this past year.

He accepted a short-notice fight against ex-champion Brandon Moreno in the lion's den of Mexico City in March and produced one of the most stunning UFC upsets in recent memory, taking the unanimous decision win in front of a hostile crowd. Kavanagh was unranked before that fight and despite more recently losing to Brandon Royval at UFC 329, he remains just a win away from breaking into the flyweight title conversation. Taking on Royval on the night of Conor McGregor's return in Las Vegas in July, Kavanagh was submitted but earned the fight of the night on one of the promotion's most-watched recent cards in a back-and-forth slugfest. The 27-year-old's exciting style and high ceiling was on show that evening and will be again when he faces Ramazonbek Temirov on what is remarkably just his second high-profile numbered event at UFC 333 on Oct. 24.

"Thinking back to certain moments [in Mexico City], it was like a rollercoaster, it was a sick opportunity and I'm glad I did it and my team backed me to do it," Kavanagh tells ESPN.

"[Royval was] another step on the journey, losing is never fun, no matter what stage you're at whether you're at the top or at any point of your career but unfortunately sometimes you have to learn like that -- learning on the go, that's what we're doing right now.

"I believe I've got the best team around me so I truly believe with this team I can make it all the way to the top and that's the plan, that's the aim.

"I'm always trying to work on things from every fight. Unfortunately, you learn a lot more when you lose."

For Kavanagh, the lights have quickly turned brighter. Like many of his British counterparts in the UFC, he was made in Cage Warriors, the organisation that can take credit for the likes of McGregor, Paddy Pimblett and Tom Aspinall. From there, a first round knockout on Dana White's Contender Series saw the journey in the big time begin. His first professional defeat came in the UFC against the experienced Charles Johnson, but that was quickly forgotten with the Moreno heist that saw his stock in the game skyrocket. Kavanagh's front-footed, devious style stemming from his kickboxing roots has even earned him praise from one of the greatest to ever step in the octagon with a Jon Jones Facetime after that UFC Mexico win leaving him "starstruck."

"Your Muay Thai is beautiful, your kicks, they don't show at all. They have no telegraph. It's so nice," Jones said to Kavanagh.

It is a style that was born at London's Great Britain Top Team (GBTT), where alongside UFC veteran Nathaniel Wood and fellow prospect Shanelle Dyer, Kavanagh has honed his craft, going from a five-time K1 kickboxing champion to now potentially a statement win away from challenging for UFC gold under British MMA trailblazer Brad Pickett. And that too in a division where the competition is possibly as fierce as it has ever been. Royval, Tatsuro Tairo, Manuel Kape, Asu Almabayev and bona fide flyweight royalty Alexandre Pantoja make up the spine of a group of challengers that Kananagh finds himself a part of.

Joshua Van's UFC 331 title defence ended any doubts about his validity as champion, with a dominant win over Pantoja, and at just 24-years-old he looks set for a stint at the top -- where Kavanagh aspires to be. But first, No. 7 ranked, one below Kavanagh, and unbeaten in the UFC, the explosive Temirov is one of the toughest challenges the Englishman has faced in his career, and in a weight class as deep as the flyweights, back-to-back losses would see Kavanagh fall mercilessly down the pecking order -- the stakes are high at UFC 333.

"I think the flyweight division is the best division at the moment. It's forever changing," Kavanagh says. "There are so many young up and comers but there are also so many people that have been around for so long. So it's got a good mixture of everything and to be honest, just excited to be a part of it - it's sick being a flyweight at this time.

"I'm a very 'one fight at a time' kind of person, I'll always look at what's in front of me and then what's next but I think it would be an exciting fight either way, [Joshua] Van vs. Lon."

Born in London to an Irish father and Chinese mother, Kavanagh wears his heritage on his sleeve with his name Lone'er translating to "Little Dragon" in English. He credits his mum for pushing him into MMA, a decision that has since paid dividends.

Kavanagh is now set to be a part of a main card alongside two title fights at the Etihad Arena in Abu Dhabi. In his way, Uzbekistan's Temirov is coming in red hot on the back of a first-round finish against Steve Erceg, he last tasted defeat in an MMA bout seven years ago and has never been knocked out.

"I haven't seen all the fighters just fighting like me. Just striking punches, just making knockouts. But my punches will just kill them all," Temirov told the UFC.

The kickboxer is aware of the danger that Temirov carries but also the opportunity up for grabs.

"I think a win there puts me right back up there. He's a dangerous opponent. He's got some good wins under him, a lot of wins, but I think a win against him puts me right back up at the top. [I'm] always looking for a finish," Kavanagh said.

"His main weapons are his heavy hands, and that excites me. I love fights like that and I think it's a good fight for me. Hopefully [another fight of the night], I'm looking for more performances of the night."

As is now customary with Kavanagh's UFC bouts, his throwdown against the formidable Temirov is one not to be missed. With the top of the flyweight division so deep he will want to turn all the excitement surrounding him into consistency to earn a shot at Van's belt, that journey will take its latest step in a treacherous division.

And as Bruce Buffer introduces both fighters, perhaps there will be something for the UFC bosses and fans alike to take away before a single punch is even thrown. That all these years after Cejudo and Johnson have been and gone, the flyweights are box office property once again.

stories.headline: Dream's Gray has minor procedure on hand ahead of Finals opener
stories.summary: Allisha Gray, who has missed the Dream's past two playoff games because of a left hand injury, is still day-to-day heading into the WNBA Finals after undergoing a minor procedure.
stories.body:
Four-time All-Star Allisha Gray underwent a minor procedure on her left hand and is still considered day-to-day for the Atlanta Dream heading into the WNBA Finals, she said Tuesday.

"Progress is great," Gray told WSB-TV when asked at practice whether she'd play in Game 1. "As of right now just day-to-day, and you'll see."

Gray did not clarify whether she had surgery on her hand, and the team declined to say when the procedure occurred.

She was seen taking shots at practice Tuesday, a day before the team travels to the Bay Area for Saturday's Finals opener against No. 2 seed Golden State.

Gray, the top scorer for the No. 4 seed Dream, has missed the past two playoff games after injuring the hand in the first half of Game 1 in a semifinal series against the New York Liberty. She was listed as questionable heading into Game 3 last Friday against New York and went through warmups before being ruled out "in the interest of caution," according to coach Karl Smesko.

The Dream advanced to the Finals with a three-game sweep.

Gray, a 6-foot guard out of South Carolina, averaged 19.0 points, 3.5 rebounds, 2.6 assists and 1.4 steals this year while appearing in all 44 regular-season games. She was also the Dream's top scorer (22.0 points per game) during their first-round sweep of the No. 5 seed Washington Mystics.

The Dream and Valkyries will both be competing for their first WNBA championship.

stories.headline: 'All love': All Blacks inspiring NZ's Rugby League World Cup tilt
stories.summary: Buoyed by a visit from their All Blacks brothers, Stacey Jones's ambitious Kiwis are out to open the rugby league World Cup with a bang by completing a memorable New Zealand double over Australia.
stories.body:
Buoyed by a visit from their All Blacks brothers, Stacey Jones's ambitious Kiwis are out to open the rugby league World Cup with a bang by completing a memorable New Zealand double over Australia.

Five days after the All Blacks crushed the Wallabies 50-19 to clinch the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year, the Kiwis and Kangaroos clash in a trans-Tasman blockbuster in Sydney on Thursday night to kick off the global showpiece.

Eight ABs, including superstar winger Will Jordan and playmaker Cam Roigard, cast aside the cross-code rivalry to drop into New Zealand's captain's run on Wednesday and throw their support behind Jones's side.

"It's just all love and supporting each other and hopefully we can go watch their game on Saturday too, so it's pretty special," New Zealand captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"How dominant and how they go about their business and represent New Zealand, there's a lot of things that they do that we look up to so yeah, it's pretty cool."

Leading what he believes is "potentially" the best Kiwi forward pack ever, Fisher-Harris says "the plan" is to lift the World Cup and, like the Warriors, continue to inspire a whole new generation of rugby league players back in their homeland just like the 2008 winners did.

"When they won in 2008, I was watching Blairy (Adam Blair) and that, (Nathan) Cayless and obviously Benji (Marshall), so that made me want to go down this path," the enforcer said.

"So hopefully we can do something like that. When you are successful like that, it gets you motivated and you want to play for a certain team or a certain code.

"So that's the plan anyways, to be successful in this World Cup."

Behind the monster pack will be Kayln Ponga for the first time after the talismanic fullback, at 28, opted to represent his parents' homeland.

"He's playing pretty good right about now," Fisher-Harris said of Ponga, who led Newcastle on their magical run from seventh to a 19-18 grand final loss to the Sydney Roosters.

"But it's not just his playing ability, it's his leadership and he's been in the game for a while now.

"He's won a few things but it looks like he's pretty keen to get in that black and white jersey."

Coach Stacey Jones also believes Australia's loss is very much New Zealand's gain.

"For the Knights this year and particularly the back end of the season, he carried them to a grand final," Jones said.

"Obviously had a lot of support around him, but he's got a lot of confidence in his game at the moment and we're just lucky that we've got him on our side."

stories.headline: Guardians start Gavin Williams vs. Rays' Griffin Jax in Game 3
stories.summary: Guardians right-hander Gavin Williams, who threw 210 pitches over six days against the White Sox, will start Game 3 of the ALCS against the Rays on Thursday.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- Guardians right-hander Gavin Williams, who threw 210 pitches over six days against the Chicago White Sox, will start Game 3 of the American League Championship Series against the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday, the club announced.

Williams, who will take the ball opposite Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, threw 11⅔ innings over three appearances in the AL Division Series against the Chicago White Sox.

He pitched five innings in Game 2 of that series before throwing 18 pitches in an inning out of the bullpen in Game 4 on two days' rest. Two days later, he posted 12 strikeouts over 5⅔ innings in Game 5 as Cleveland came back from an 0-2 deficit to advance to the ALCS.

"I feel like that was kind of a normal workload for me, except throwing in the game for my pen session," Williams said. "But nothing really. Body feels good. Arm feels good. And going to go out there tomorrow."

Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti said Williams threw a bullpen Tuesday in Tampa Bay before the club settled on him starting Game 3.

"We just wanted to see how he responded to the workload to determine when the best time for him to pitch in the series would be," Antonetti said.

Williams, 27, finished the regular season with a 3.76 ERA and an AL-leading 248 strikeouts in 184⅓ innings over 32 starts. He will take the mound Thursday earlier than expected after Major League Baseball moved the start time for Game 3 up from 6 p.m. to 1 p.m. ET with rain in the forecast for Northeast Ohio later in the day.

The change could benefit Williams if the regular season is any indication; he had a 4.82 ERA in 19 night starts and a 2.42 ERA in 13 day starts.

"I feel like I'm very routine-oriented," Williams said. "I wake up about the same time every day, no matter if it's a night game or a day game. I honestly stick to my routines throughout the whole day. I know the process of warming up changes from a day game to a night game, but everything else in between stays the same."

Jax's postseason workload, meanwhile, has consisted of a single two-inning relief outing in Game 3 of the ALDS against the New York Yankees. The converted reliever will make his first career postseason start on seven days' rest from that appearance, in which he allowed a run, walked one and struck out four. It will be his first start since logging three scoreless innings Sept. 26 against the Philadelphia Phillies in an outing that was cut short after he took a line drive off his lower back.

"It's a big honor, one that I've been looking forward to for a really long time now that I'm in the rotation," Jax said. "Didn't work out in the division series, but I was just happy to pitch any single role I could have. But here now, in a seven-game series, looking forward to helping this team, starting this game."

Jax, 31, was one of baseball's best relievers when the Rays acquired him from the Minnesota Twins at the trade deadline last season. He opened this season as a reliever before beginning his transition to the rotation at the end of April. He compiled a 3.14 ERA in 23 starts compared with an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances.

"What we like is what he's done as a starter for us all season long," Rays manager Kevin Cash said. "A lot of confidence with him. It's really good stuff. He gets it in the zone. Gets himself in rhythm. I think he's done a tremendous job of transitioning into that starter routine and just go do what he's done."

stories.headline: UCL talking points, MD2: Who's to blame for Man United mess? Chaos bad for Madrid?
stories.summary: Which players and clubs shined in the Champions League? Gab Marcotti, Tom Hamilton and Sam Marsden weigh in on all the moments that mattered from Matchday 2.
stories.body:
The UEFA Champions League returned with a big Matchday 2 this week, with blockbuster results up and down the league phase table and a whopping 78 goals across the 18 games: an average of 4.33 per game. Liverpool and Aston Villa scooped up big wins, Manchester City were humbled at home by Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona and Real Madrid overturned road deficits to win in fine/dramatic fashion, and Bayern Munich scrambled to a 3-3 draw at minnows Viking in one of the wilder results of the round.

What to make of it all? ESPN FC writers Gab Marcotti, Sam Marsden and Tom Hamilton are here to break down the action.

- Reaction: Man City can't compete with PSG, Europe's gold standard

- Kirkland: Real Madrid fight back, but a trophy seems far from reach

- Ogden: Blame for Man United malaise shouldn't fall on Carrick

Q1. Manchester United conceded in the first minute at Atletico Madrid and it didn't get any better from there, with the 2-0 defeat followed by something even worse: a player (Lisandro Martínez) calling out executives (in this case, Jason Wilcox) for their shoddy work in the summer. The club is a mess from top to bottom, and manager Michael Carrick is surely feeling the heat. Can he coach them through this, or is the club's best hope yet another early-season reset?

Tom Hamilton: It all depends how reactionary the executives are, and how sure they are in themselves and the plan they've put forward. The club has an astonishing ability of making poor decisions -- both on the field and off it -- but given they backed Michael Carrick with a two-year contract in May, unless they have a ready-made replacement lined up (Kieran McKenna, Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte or Julian Nagelsmann perhaps) there's little point changing the management. As Martinez said (though the players cannot remotely be absolved of blame here), the recruitment left the club short-changed: where's the left-back cover? Where's a 20-goal-a-season striker? Of the players they've signed, only Carlos Baleba looks like an improvement on what they had last season.

That said, unless there's improvement sooner rather than later, when the heat is on those in the corridors of power, to quote Logan Roy, often they decide it's "time for a blood sacrifice." If they pull this lever, the identity of the fall guy will be fascinating.

Martinez's rant could have a galvanising effect on the team and if that happens, then morale and results will improve. But if the team continue to underwhelm on the pitch -- and let's face it, their fixture list so far has been relatively kind -- then expect some kind of reckoning.

Gab Marcotti: Lisandro Martinez is part of the problem (note the way he defended Dominic Solanke at the weekend), but his words could be part of the solution. Many are reading it as simply him being unhappy with the signings in the summer and making it all about Wilcox. But it goes beyond that.

There's a sense of drift at United, and that really shouldn't be the case given the manager has been in charge for less than a year. So all we get is Carrick talking, and he's not the most inspiring figure. All he says -- rightly, from his perspective -- is how they finished last season strong and they want to build on it and it will take time. And while it's true they finished third, they didn't play particularly well, and a lot of it had to do with the Premier League's other big clubs changing managers. (It's not a coincidence that Liverpool, Spurs and Chelsea all have new guys in charge.)

That message only takes you so far. Somebody needs to speak up (other than Carrick) and offer some accountability.

Why did they make the choices they made? What are their plans? What is the long-term thinking? And maybe get that across to the players too. Maybe it's Wilcox talking, maybe it's CEO Omar Berrada, maybe somebody else. But right now, the only message United fans (and players) are getting is from Carrick (dull and repetitive, but not really his fault) and from the pitch (bad).

Sam Marsden: United are in the same spiral they have been in for a decade. From the outside looking in, they're already damned if they do, damned if they don't this season because the squad is so far behind Europe's elite. Sticking with Carrick or sacking him is not going to change that any time soon. If I could explain in 100 words how they get back on track immediately, I would probably be wanted by the biggest clubs on the continent, but one thing remains as clear as ever: the problem starts at the top (ownership, director of football etc) and not with the coach or the players.

Q2. Barcelona rallied from a losing position to yet again romp to a big win, this time over Galatasaray, 4-1 away from home. We're worried about Lamine Yamal -- 13 starts for club and country in the last seven weeks makes us worry he's going to burn out before the business end of the season -- but more than that, Barca are still averaging over four goals per game this long into the 2026-27 campaign. Are they ever going to slow down? Can anyone slow them down?

Hamilton: Not yet. Even when they went behind in the cauldron of the Ali Sami Yen Stadium, they barely blinked. Lamine Yamal could well end up being crowned the world's best player at the end of October when the Ballon d'Or winner is announced, but his form seems to be building game on game. His two assists were just spellbinding: the first a beautifully weighted cross to find Fermín López and then came a befuddling piece of skill as he danced past Eren Elmali to tee up Anthony Gordon. It's clicking nicely. "We played against players who know each other by heart," Galatasaray manager Okan Buruk said afterwards. "They are like a complete machine."

There are longer-term concerns around the workload. FIFPRO's briefing before the World Cup was alarming to say the least: players are at a greater risk of burnout than ever before, so Yamal's minutes need to be managed. This is, in theory, where the strength of their squad and Hansi Flick's juggling skills will be managed.

Barca are in their rhythm now, but the next five or so weeks will tell us a huge amount. They have Real Betis away on Saturday, then a trip to PSG next Tuesday before El Clasico and Real Madrid on Oct. 25. Aston Villa and Atletico are also waiting in November.

Marsden: I wouldn't expect much rest for Yamal soon. It's already clear the rules are different for him. He was the only Spain player to start all four games in the international break, and he continues to be overused by Barcelona.

Getafe last weekend would have been the perfect game to rest him ahead of the run Barça have coming up. He could at least have come off once Barça scored their fourth in Istanbul. Instead, you presume because he had not scored in either game, Flick left him on.

Perhaps the German coach didn't want to tinker with the attack too much after being left without the injured Raphinha, but his claim about more minutes being better for Yamal when training between games is not so intense doesn't seem to apply to any other squad member. That said, maybe he just leaves him on because he's so fun to watch.

Like Tom said, that assist for Gordon's goal -- admittedly with a bit of luck -- was beautiful. If he's not the best player in the game right now, he's definitely the most fun. As for Barça, 43 goals in 10 games is a joke and they look superb, but let's hold off on anointing them the best team in the world for now. Next week's matches against PSG and Madrid will reveal a lot.

Marcotti: Yeah, I'm with Marsden here. The toughest challenges they've had thus far are Galatasaray away, Sevilla away and Athletic Bilbao at home. And without wanting to be overly mean, Galatasaray lost 4-0 to Trabzonspor heading into the break, while Sevilla had a bumpy summer (again) and Athletic Bilbao are mid-table. I'd suggest it's the next three games -- Betis (third in La Liga) away, PSG away and the Clasico -- that will tell us whether they really are this record-breaking juggernaut or whether they're merely very good.

That said, I don't see how Yamal's minutes can be good for him, mentally or physically. I hope Marsden's wrong when he suggests Flick left him on because he hadn't yet scored. Barcelona no doubt have a top sport science team who know what they're doing so I guess you have to trust in them.

Maybe he really is some sort of machine. But from the outside it doesn't look great.

Q3. Paris Saint-Germain delivered a dose of schadenfreude for Man City's critics on Wednesday, cruising to a 3-0 lead early and making the hosts look ordinary. PSG's results have been dire in Ligue 1 so far this season, but manager Luis Enrique has insisted that this team is better than last year's. Do we think he's right, and will they do a three-peat in Europe?

Marsden: To answer the questions, yes and, probably, yes. The second is far from a given, of course, but they are huge favourites to win the Champions League. Not necessarily because of this win over Manchester City, mind. That three-goal lead and the eventual win flattered them in Manchester. City created and wasted far more chances, while PSG -- helped by their former goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma -- were much more effective in front of goal.

If we have learned one thing from the last two years, though, it's not to judge PSG until spring. Luis Enrique doesn't take Ligue 1 seriously for months, fully aware that he can rest players, risk results and still win the league by running into form at the right time. Case in point is Ousmane Dembélé, who was given the weekend off to prepare for City -- he played 76 minutes, notching a goal and an assist -- and has started just three league games this season.

That said, despite downplaying anything that happens to PSG pre-Christmas, can I just shock you? Next week's game against Barcelona in Paris is the standout game of the league phase and the winners will absolutely, definitely go on to win the Champions League. Maybe.

Hamilton: I'm not sure if Sam was intending that Oasis pastiche, but I loved it. To be able to rest one of the world's best players (Khvicha Kvaratshkelia) and still dispatch a fired-up Manchester City, while taking any sting out of the emotion of the occasion, was testament to the champions mindset Luis Enrique has built at PSG. And Sam is right - they have the luxury of being able to operate in second gear for the start of the season in Ligue 1 and then spring into life when needed.

What Luis Enrique has achieved at PSG is to keep the team continually evolving. At some point they'll inevitably translate that over in the French league too. Europe will be on notice. That Barcelona game will be box office.

Marcotti: I'm going to dissent a little bit. I don't think PSG vastly outplayed City; there were individual errors from the home team and individual moments of genius from the visitors. Take out Ferran Torres' meaningless missed penalty and City actually won the xG battle by a whopping 2.57 to 1.05. It doesn't mean PSG's victory wasn't deserved, but I think it does mean there isn't some massive gulf in class between them.

That said, in terms of talent, PSG are definitely better than last year going forward in the sense that they have more solutions. Ferran Torres is probably a better fit than Gonçalo Ramos. Maghnes Akliouche, in my view, is an upgrade on Bradley Barcola, and Mika Godts is hugely exciting. The midfield also should be getting better just by inertia as these guys grow: Warren Zaïre-Emery is 20, João Neves 22, Dro 18. Vitinha, at 26, is in his prime.

It's at the back where, maybe, you could quibble. I'm not a Matvei Safonov guy (at all) in goal, while Marquinhos is getting older. In terms of depth, Lucas Beraldo and Ilya Zabarnyi are nothing to write home about. All that said, on the other hand, one more season metabolizing Luis Enrique's brand of football: that's huge. So maybe they are better.

Q4. Jose Mourinho has taken many of the headlines since returning to Real Madrid, but their frankly incredible comeback -- from 3-1 down at Roma to 4-3 winners in the final 10 minutes -- should put a little spotlight on the team after a largely woeful display. Endrick (goal, assist) and Arda Güler (two assists) came on at the hour mark and turned the game. Is this level of chaos on and off the field going to help this team in the long run, or hurt it?

Marsden: I think that in the long run, the chaos will hurt Real Madrid. Roma were as poor at defending their lead -- and set pieces -- late on as they were impressive in taking the game to Madrid before then. Not all opposition will be as generous to Mourinho as his former team were. The banners of gratitude for the Portuguese coach before the game were one thing; conceding three goals between the 83rd and 90th minute was something else entirely.

As for Madrid, it is telling that it was substitutes Endrick, Guler and Carlos Espí who helped swing the game in their favour. Other than perhaps Guler, it's hard to advocate for any of them to be regular starters, but the fact they showed up in Rome once again places question marks on whether Madrid's big name stars can all function together. Kylian Mbappé, once again on target here, and Jude Bellingham have produced moments this season, but Vinícius Júnior is still off the boil. The Brazilian, hooked after an hour in Italy, is without a goal for his club in eight games. It is getting harder and harder to make a case for him to be in Madrid's best XI.

Luckily for Mourinho, it's a problem he can park for now. Vinicius has been banned for four league games after being sent off for a hair pull in the win over Villarreal at the weekend. The picture could be very different by the time he's available for selection again if Madrid click without him.

Marcotti: The chaos hurts, of course it does. Real Madrid were at full strength against a Roma side without their first-choice keeper (it kinda showed) and who lost Manu Koné after 15 minutes and Paulo Dybala at half-time. In the 79th minute, they were losing 3-1, had managed a paltry 0.35 xG and three shots on target.

Mourinho is more comfortable than most in chaos, but that doesn't mean he'd rather choose chaos than coherence. When, at the hour mark, you're 3-0 down and you send on Endrick -- who had played five minutes of football this season and last started for the club in May 2025 -- you're definitely sending a message. (Not just to Vinicius, either...)

It's tempting to have sympathy for Mourinho when you take a step back because this team was built not with an idea of football in mind, but rather as a collection of Panini stickers. That's not down to him. On the other hand, some of his antics -- and the fact that club president Florentino Perez will neither hold him to account nor take any steps to actually build a team, rather than a collection of stars (just ask Alvaro Arbeloa or Xabi Alonso) -- makes it hard to have too much sympathy.

A word on Roma, while we're at it. They had a tougher time against Como than they did against Real Madrid. Conceding goals like that is frustrating and unacceptable, but the first 80-odd minutes were something else...

Hamilton: Real Madrid, Perez and Mourinho all knew what they were getting when they took a collective step forward into this latest marriage. Mourinho was fully aware of the team he was inheriting and the plans to develop it. Perez knew he was getting back a much-loved coach, who has a tendency to spontaneously combust but also possesses a rare dab of magic and retains an aura. So it's no surprise that there's an element of footballing chaos.

There is always drama around Madrid and Mourinho: bringing the two together is like leaving Rambo and John McClane on a desert island together and asking them to build a raft. It could sink, or it could lead to a fine old ship getting back on course. Perhaps chaos is the way to destabilise the Barcelona machine. Either way, it's going to be box office.

After being abject for so much of the match, Mourinho got his substitutes right and they changed the game. If you look closely, there's usually order inside chaos anyway.

Q5. OK, dealer's choice. What else stood out to you in a goal-heavy Matchday 2?

Hamilton: Heading into the Fenerbahce match, Aston Villa's form had been poor this season, without a single home win. But that's to be expected after a summer of mass change both on and off the field. The North Stand is under redevelopment. A grand total of five people were dotted around the vast empty bank on Wednesday night: four builders on the night shift, and one camera operator high up in the last remaining seats waiting to be removed. It's all part of Villa's push to take the ground's capacity to over 50,000, but there's been a rebuilding job both on and off the pitch in recent times.

But against Fenerbahce, it all came together. Nicolas Jackson and Johan Manzambi were exceptional, while Fenerbahce looked tired and off the pace as Villa swiped them aside 6-0. Manzambi was a constant threat and opened the scoring, while Jackson grabbed two more before the break. Ross Barkley scored twice in the second half with Tammy Abraham adding a sixth. This will have brought joy to manager Unai Emery, who is overseeing this rebuild after a summer in which the team said goodbye to Ollie Watkins, Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne, Emi Martinez and Youri Tielemens. The new-look Villa is starting to purr, with the brilliant Manzambi at the heart of this side.

Marsden: Look away now if you're Serie A as it was a miserable week for all the Italian sides. It started on Tuesday with defensive horror shows from Inter and Napoli. Inter leaked four at home as they were beaten 4-3 by Club Brugge -- shout out to the Belgian side's striker, Nicolo Tresoldi, who scored a hat-trick and will probably move to a bigger club soon -- and Napoli lost 3-1 at Villarreal. It's zero points for both teams, the last two Scudetto winners, after two games.

Things didn't get much better on Wednesday. Como were beaten 3-2 by Feyenoord and Roma, as discussed above, crumbled from a winning position to lose 4-3 to Madrid. So, four games, four losses and 14 goals conceded for the Serie A sides this week. Como did at least start with a win and Roma have a point, so it's not all doom and gloom. You would imagine all four teams are too good to not finish in at least the top 24, but it's a worrying start. The next few match weeks will be interesting.

Marcotti: I'm giving a shout out to Sabah, who won their first ever Champions League game, beating Slavia Prague 2-0. I'm not going to bore you with how their coach, Valdas Dambrauskas, won the Lithuanian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire," used the money to move to London, study sports science and get his coaching badges. By now, unless you've been living under a rock you've probably heard the story.

Nor am I going to point out that they were only founded in 2017 and yet have unseated perennial Azerbaijani powerhouse Qarabag domestically. It's quite a feat, sure, but they also have a very wealthy owner who spent a ton on club facilities and hired the right kinds of nerds to do the analytics and recruitment.

Rather, I'd like to highlight how the Champions League manages to be, at once, the sort of space where superclubs like Manchester City and PSG can duke it out alongside Sabah and Slavia Prague. Let it be a reminder that the more you spend, the more there are diminishing returns. And just because your budget is 10x somebody else's doesn't mean you're 10x more likely to win.

stories.headline: Love (ankle) sits out Cardinals practice as LaFleur says rest 'vital'
stories.summary: Arizona Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love didn't practice Wednesday to rest his ailing left ankle. His status for Sunday's game against the Rams isn't clear.
stories.body:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Arizona Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love did not practice Wednesday to rest his ailing left ankle and his status for Sunday's game against the Rams isn't clear as of yet, coach Mike LaFleur said.

The plan, LaFleur said, is to take Love's ankle "one day at a time," but the Cardinals understand for it to fully heal, the third-overall pick needs to stay off it.

"We all are in agreeance as much as he wants to battle through, we're all in agreeance right now, it's just, hey just give it a little bit of rest and see as the week goes on what that'll entail for Sunday."

Love's style of play, however, makes it difficult for him to prevent the injury from lingering, LaFleur intimated.

"I'm going to try to be as candid as possible with also knowing that everyone's listening to this, too," LaFleur said, "but he's a tough dude. "

But you guys see the way he plays and how aggressive he is with his cuts. And, I mean, imagine being a back in the NFL trying to put the foot down and cut the way that you're capable of?"

Asked whether he was concerned about Love's injury lingering, LaFleur swiftly pointed out which body part was injured.

"They're ankles. It's an ankle," LaFleur said. "So, you don't know. I'm not a doctor and each body's a little bit different. The way he came back from the one in the preseason was unbelievable. I mean, he doesn't even feel it. But this one is the one that happened when the regular season started and it's just lingered."

Love has rushed for 245 yards and one touchdown on 67 carries this season for an average of 3.7 yards per carry. He's also contributed 36 receiving yards and a touchdown on 11 catches. His best game to date came in Week 3 at San Francisco, when he ran for 89 yards.

The Notre Dame star rushed for just 22 yards in Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions on 12 carries.

LaFleur said, in some ways, Love's explosiveness has been affected by the ankle injury in recent weeks.

"You'd have to ask him that," LaFleur said. "I know how explosive he is. I know how explosive he wants to be. So, I mean, I think that's a fair assessment in some aspects. Again, I don't think it's an overall hindrance, but again, the rest for him is going to be vital."

stories.headline: 'I'm a competitor': Cody Walker primed and ready for the next step
stories.summary: Cody Walker has lived a year of Carlton's ups and downs before having even been drafted. He's learned a lot about the business of footy and what he needs to do to take the next step, as his own AFL career begins.
stories.body:
Cody Walker had a front row seat to Carlton's tumultuous season. In line meetings, at team dinners, out of the Michael Voss era and into the Josh Fraser fairytale. From door stops to crisis meetings, it was an eye opening introduction to the big business of footy for the son-of-a-gun.

"I actually reflect on it a bit now and consider how low a club can get. Being on the inside with all the outside noise that we had when all the Vossy stuff was going down, it was really quite interesting to see," Walker tells ESPN.

"Then going from that to top of the AFL and beating Brisbane and Fremantle towards the end of the season, seeing how good a club can feel and get. For that to both happen in one season I find it quite interesting. I'm sort of glad it happened in a way that I get to experience both worlds."

In the midst of their early season malaise, Blues players were subjected to abuse walking off the ground after second half fadeouts and even rocked up to Ikon Park with anti-Voss graffiti on the club walls. That included Walker as he trained full-time with the squad.

"All the outside noise tears you apart a little bit. To see fans out the front of Ikon Park sort of giving it to you, and open training to have people yelling out at you and it's your fans, they've got Carlton stuff on, but they're yelling out to you, it's pretty full on."

From 1-8 under Voss, the Blues stormed home under Fraser, winning their next six starts and claiming a remarkable win in a wildcard final against Melbourne.

A fractured playing group was united under a first-time head coach and Walker was along for the ride.

"It was quite an eye opener how sad it can get inside a club. You sort of have to keep to yourself in those moments and just get around the boys," he says.

"We definitely had to stick together as a group, and Fraser's been really good at that. We did a lot together this year, the players grabbed me along to every dinner they had. It was so good, such a good experience."

That finals finish means Carlton receives no discount on matching a bid on the son of high-flyer Andrew, with the pair likely to become the first father-son duo to each be selected in the top five of an AFL Draft.

Walker's talent deserves to see him taken at pick 2, just like his dad.

An electric midfielder blessed with the twitchiness, agility and burst to free himself from stoppages, Walker enjoyed a brilliant campaign with Carlton's VFL side and cemented his status in the 2026 draft.

There's no doubting his mercurial talent and its fit alongside Patrick Cripps, Sam Walsh, and Jagga Smith, but Walker isn't yet the complete package, and he's the first one to acknowledge it.

"I think my burst out of stoppage and ball-winning is my 'one wood'... when I look back on footage and see for myself how dangerous I can look going out of stoppage, it's really eye-opening for me," he tells ESPN.

"My improvements I want going into next year, I want to improve every part of my fundamentals. I've got a little bit of disposal efficiency which can let me down, but I'll put a power of work into kicking and handballing.

"It got to the point where I was doing two or three sessions a week, and that includes Diesel Williams helping me out.

"I've got so many good people around me and I can already feel that I'm getting better at those things. I'm pretty straightforward in what I want to get better at and I like getting harsh feedback from coaches that I can work on.

"No one's really pissing in my pocket about something I need to work on and I don't realise it until I'm maybe on [the MCG] one day and it's a problem for me if I'm missing kicks or missing handballs."

Walker's final game before he turns professional wasn't in Carlton's VFL side, at the national championships with Vic Country or back with the Bendigo Pioneers. It was in the Goulburn Valley Football League playing for hometown Echuca, and he spent most of his lead-up convincing the Blues' General Manager of Football to let him go.

"I actually sat down with Chris Davies about two weeks before the granny. I was like, 'What are the chances I get to play?'" Walker recalls to ESPN.

"He was like, 'Mate, we're not going to stop you. Preferably, I think it's the wrong decision, but it's all your choice.'"

Walker was determined to enjoy one more stint out in the country with his best mates after a massive top-age season, but injured his ankle during training the week after that conversation with Davies. It ruled him out of the qualifying final, but he still had an eye towards their qualification into the big dance.

"I went home for two weeks and I was training with Echuca and I just got addicted. I called up the club and a few people there and I was like 'I think I'm going to play, I'm doing it'. I'm so glad I did it."

Walker had 20 disposals, eight score involvements, and kicked a goal off the wing in Echuca's 13-goal win over the Shepparton Swans.

It underlined the values that have made Walker rise and rise through junior football ranks. His competitive spirit and genuine love of footy through rich bloodlines continually stands out. Carlton supporters have known of Walker's footballing exploits for years, but they may not know what makes him tick.

That attitude was on show in the 2km time trial at the AFL Draft combine. Walker led his group of runners by the length of the straight, finishing nine seconds ahead of second place. It's his inner motivation that drives him to compete against the best, and oftentimes that means competing against himself.

It's why he has a grin on his face when asked why he even ran despite some Blues supporters bemoaning his name rising higher on rival clubs' draft boards.

"It was probably to beat my [personal best]... my PB was 6:13, I was feeling good and I had a bit in the tank," he says.

"Personally I'm a competitor. I do want to see where I'm at as of right now compared to maybe three months later when I do a 2k at the club."

Walker smashed that time, finishing in 6:04 minutes and on the podium despite running in a slower pack.

It's given Carlton more to consider, lacking the points to match a bid at pick 1 but desperate to secure its second elite father-son prospect in as many years after Harry Dean was taken with pick two in 2025.

"I've got plenty of trust in the club with what they can do in my scenario," Walker says.

"I love the Carlton Football Club and I'm really thankful they've given me this year and it would be a really cool thing to end up at my dad's club. There's a lot of history there."

stories.headline: Lisandro Martínez: I believe in 'everyone working to help' Man United 'move forward'
stories.summary: Lisandro Martínez has said he believes in "my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward."
stories.body:
Lisandro Martínez has said he believes in "my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward" after he criticised Manchester United's hierarchy, including director of football Jason Wilcox, in an explosive interview on Tuesday.

Following United's 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, Martínez told Amazon Prime that he felt the club had failed to adequately strengthen the squad during the summer transfer window.

But, in a statement published to social media on Wednesday, the Argentine defender said that responsibility also lies with himself and with his teammates to improve the club's fortunes.

"When I talk about wanting more, I'm talking about the ambition we must all have as part of this club," Martínez said. "To keep growing, to become stronger and to have everything we need to compete at the highest level. These are standards we must all hold ourselves to, starting with me.

"I know that, first and foremost, it's us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility. We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take Manchester United back to the top.

"I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward. I'm convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment.

"My goal has been the same since day one, to win, to compete at the highest level and to give everything I have for this badge."

Sources told ESPN on Wednesday that United were assessing whether to take disciplinary action against the 28-year-old, who said in his statement that he "spoke out of anger and frustration at not getting the result we all wanted.

"Those who know me know how I live football, with passion, commitment and a huge desire to win.

"And when things don't go our way, it hurts, especially when representing a club with the history and stature of Manchester United.

"My words reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours.

"Those high standards are part of how I see football and the responsibility that comes with wearing this shirt."

- Sources: Man United assessing Lisandro Martínez comments

- Martínez exposes Man United's harsh reality: Blame lies with top brass, not Carrick

- Wayne Rooney: Lisandro Martinez 'disrespectful' for Man United rant

United have won just two of their nine games this season: a 5-2 Premier League victory over Ipswich Town in August and a 4-0 win over Sabah FK in the Champions League in mid-September.

They spent £150 million ($199m) on Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans during the summer transfer window.

Sources told ESPN that Wilcox retains the support of United chiefs.

ESPN's Rob Dawson contributed to reporting.

Fifty-nine years ago today was the start of a new era in the NHL. In the 1967-68 season, the league doubled in size, adding the California Seals, Los Angeles Kings, Minnesota North Stars, Philadelphia Flyers, Pittsburgh Penguins and St. Louis Blues in the new West Division, with the Original Six franchises making up the East Division.

On Oct. 14, 1967, two of those new teams -- the Kings and the Flyers -- would meet for the their NHL debuts at California's Long Beach Arena. The Kings won 4-2, with Brian Kilrea scoring both the historic first goal in franchise history as well as an empty-netter to seal the deal.

Each team has gone on to win two Stanley Cups in the time since -- 1974 and 1975 for the Flyers, and 2012 and 2014 for the Kings -- but the franchises have never met in a postseason series.

stories.headline: Christian Horner: Mercedes' Toto Wolff has it 'easy' at the moment
stories.summary: Former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner has suggested that Mercedes boss Toto Wolff has "got it quite easy" at the moment.
stories.body:
Former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner has suggested that Mercedes boss Toto Wolff has "got it quite easy" at the moment.

Horner, 52, officially left Red Bull Racing in September last year having been relieved of "operational duties" following last July's British Grand Prix. It ended a 20-year career with the team, where he won eight drivers' and six constructors' titles.

The past decade saw Horner spar with Wolff as Red Bull and Mercedes did battle.

This season, Horner's old team are currently fourth in the constructors' standings with 11 podiums and two wins, both claimed by Max Verstappen during this month's races in Bahrain and Singapore.

Mercedes top the constructors' leaderboard, while Kimi Antonelli is first in the drivers' standings having won eight races so far.

A potential return to F1 for Horner remains a hot topic and in an interview earlier this year, Wolff suggested Horner had "broken a lot of glass."

In an interview with the Guardian, Horner said: "He [Wolff] also said this [Red Bull] engine was going to be completely s--t and a disaster.

"Toto's got it quite easy at the moment. Zak Brown [head of McLaren] is compromised because he's using Toto's engine so he can't ruffle feathers.

"All sport needs rivalry, whether it's [Alex] Ferguson and [Arsene] Wenger, [Jose] Mourinho and (Pep) Guardiola. It percolates and polarises. I used that to galvanise good people to take on Mercedes."

- Formula 1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Toto Wolff finds quirky solution to Kimi Antonelli track limits 'stress'

Horner also revealed in the interview that he has suffered from panic attacks and has worked to recognise the symptoms.

"I didn't know what it was. You suddenly feel dizzy and conscious of your breathing and you think there's something strange going on. I put it down to having had too much coffee on an oppressive, muggy, thundery day," he said.

"Then it happened again. I got checked out and there was nothing physically the matter. They said: 'We think you have anxiety. Your breathing's very shallow.' It was my body telling me you're pushing pretty hard here. I'm able to recognise the symptoms now and let it go, and breathe."

stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.

Brendan Allen fought a back-and-forth battle with Christian Leroy Duncan in Saturday's UFC Fight Night main event. Going into the fifth round of the meeting of top-10 middleweights, Allen was narrowly ahead on all three scorecards. Of course, he did not know what the judges were thinking.

So Allen took it out of the judges' hands in Round 5, getting Duncan to the ground and efficiently finishing the gritty fight with a rear-naked choke.

With his fourth straight victory, Allen moves up one spot to No. 5 in the ESPN divisional rankings, continuing his recent climb in the middleweight top 10.

stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."
